sources.title: Disaggregated Serving (NVIDIA Dynamo Documentation)

facts.claim: Dynamo uses NIXL to transfer KV cache directly from prefill-engine VRAM to decode-engine VRAM, non-blocking

sources.title: DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving

disagreements.topic: When does prefill/decode disaggregation actually pay off?

positions.claim: Disaggregation is close to a strict win for goodput under fixed TTFT/TPOT SLOs: DistServe shows 7.4x more requests or 12.6x tighter SLO than colocated systems on A100s; Mooncake reports up to 525% throughput and 75% more real-world requests; TensorRT-LLM measures 1.4x-6.11x speedups on GB200 depending on ISL:OSL ratio.

In production TCO terms on current hardware, disaggregation's advantage is conditional on the interactivity (tok/s/user) target: GB200 NVL72 with disaggregated prefill beats single 8-GPU B200 nodes only below about 90 tok/s/user; above that crossover, the simpler aggregated 8-GPU B200 server wins on TCO per million tokens.

disagreements.topic: Is a second (decode) pool worth the operational cost, or does chunked-prefill on a single colocated engine capture most of the benefit?

positions.claim: Disaggregation is necessary: colocating prefill and decode causes measurable prefill-decode interference (DistServe measures decoding slowdown with each added prefill job) and chunked-prefill only mitigates, does not eliminate, this interference while adding O(N^2) redundant KV-cache HBM reads for N prefill chunks. Mooncake explicitly reconsidered the question after chunked-prefill became common and chose to keep disaggregation for long-context multi-node prefill and VRAM-saving reasons.

vLLM's default production path is a single colocated engine with continuous batching and chunked-prefill (with disaggregation offered only as an explicitly 'experimental' KV-connector feature) — implying that for many deployments the added complexity of a second pool, a KV transport layer, and cross-pool scheduling is not (yet) considered worth it outside of large-scale or SLO-critical deployments.

disagreements.topic: How large should the cross-node decode expert-parallel degree be for a DeepSeek-class MoE model?

positions.claim: DeepSeek-V3's own December 2024 technical report specifies a decode minimum deployment unit of EP320 across 40 nodes (320 GPUs), each GPU hosting exactly one expert, with 64 GPUs dedicated to redundant/shared experts.

DeepSeek's own February 2025 Open Source Week disclosure describes production decode running at EP144 across only 18 nodes (144 GPUs), each GPU hosting 2 routed experts plus 1 shared expert — a much smaller unit reached after roughly two months of operating the service.

Approximate prefix-cache scoring (fixed-size block hashing plus an in-memory LRU index of recently-routed prefixes) is cheap, scales with fleet size without a synchronous global state, and is llm-d's default scheduling mode.

Precise KV-cache indexing subscribes to real KV cache add/evict events emitted by vLLM (and SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) over ZeroMQ and maintains an exact, globally consistent view of which token blocks live on which pod — correct at the cost of an event-streaming subsystem and tokenization round-trips to the engine.
